lesson.title: Powering the Proton Pump: The Chloroplast Electron Transport Chain
lesson.summary: The chloroplast electron transport chain moves electrons from Photosystem II to Photosystem I through a series of redox reactions that pump protons into the thylakoid lumen, powering ATP synthase to generate ATP.
lesson.body:
The electron transport chain that links Photosystem II to Photosystem I is where the light dependent reactions convert redox chemistry into a usable proton gradient, and ultimately into ATP. Each carrier molecule in the chain has a slightly different tendency to hold onto electrons, so electrons move through the sequence in a directional, energetically favorable series of oxidation reduction reactions, each carrier being reduced as it accepts an electron and oxidized as it hands that electron to the next carrier in line.

The sequence begins when the primary electron acceptor of Photosystem II passes its electron to plastoquinone, a small, lipid soluble carrier that can move freely within the thylakoid membrane. Plastoquinone picks up not just electrons but also protons from the stroma side of the membrane, then delivers its electron to the cytochrome b6f complex, a large multi protein assembly that functions much like the analogous complex found in mitochondrial electron transport. As cytochrome b6f passes the electron onward, it releases the protons plastoquinone was carrying into the thylakoid lumen and actively translocates additional protons across the membrane, directly building the proton concentration gradient that powers ATP synthesis.

From cytochrome b6f, the electron passes to plastocyanin, a small, water soluble copper containing protein that shuttles through the thylakoid lumen to deliver the electron to Photosystem I's oxidized P700 reaction center, restoring the electron it lost when absorbing its own photon. By this point, the thylakoid lumen has become significantly more acidic and proton rich than the surrounding stroma, both from protons pumped by cytochrome b6f and from the protons released directly by water splitting at Photosystem II, creating a substantial electrochemical gradient across the thylakoid membrane.

That gradient represents stored potential energy, and the thylakoid membrane contains an enzyme, ATP synthase, that allows protons to flow back down their concentration gradient from the lumen into the stroma through a channel built into the enzyme itself. As protons pass through, the enzyme's structure rotates and drives the phosphorylation of ADP into ATP, adding a third phosphate group and, with it, the high energy phosphoanhydride bond that defines ATP's structure and makes it such a useful, readily hydrolyzed energy currency for the rest of the cell. This process, generating ATP using light driven proton gradients, is called photophosphorylation.

The ATP produced here in the stroma, together with the NADPH generated when electrons finally reach Photosystem I and are passed to NADP+ reductase, are the two products the entire light dependent apparatus, pigments, photosystems, water splitting, and this electron transport chain, exists to generate. Both molecules diffuse into the surrounding stroma, where the Calvin cycle uses their stored energy and reducing power to fix carbon dioxide into sugar, completing the link from a captured photon at the start of this concept sequence to a stable, storable molecule of food.
